title: Blood lead secular trend in a cohort of children in Mexico City (1987-2002).
ehr_evidence: We extracted air lead information from the Statistical Compendium of the System of Atmospheric Monitoring of the Metropolitan Zone of the Valley of Mexico (MZVM), 1986–2002.
summary: Prospective cohort study evaluating secular trends in blood lead levels and environmental exposures in children born in Mexico City from 1987 to 1992 over their first 10 years of life.
key_findings: Yearly mean air lead decreased from 2.80 µg/m³ in 1987 to 0.07 µg/m³ in 2002.
Each natural log decrease in air lead was accompanied by a 23.7% decrease in blood lead concentration for children born in 1987, falling to nearly zero for those born in 1992.
Geometric mean blood lead rose from 8.4 µg/dL (95% CI, 7.7 to 9.2) at 1 year to 10.1 µg/dL (95% CI, 9.3 to 11.0) at 2 years, then decreased to 6.4 µg/dL (95% CI, 5.8 to 7.1) at 10 years.
Children from the lowest socioeconomic stratum had 32.3% (95% CI, 17.0 to 49.5) higher geometric mean blood lead than the highest stratum.
Children from families using lead-glazed ceramics had 18.5% (95% CI, 10.0 to 27.6) higher geometric mean blood lead than nonusers.
Children living in the northeast sector had 10.9% (95% CI, 2.4 to 18.6) higher geometric mean blood lead than those in the southwest.
Significant decrease (p < 0.01) in the percentage of children with blood lead ≥ 10 µg/dL across year of birth during the first 7 years of life.
captured_features: complete vs incomplete blood lead data
data_source_type: prospective cohort / biospecimen assays / environmental monitoring
population: 321 children born in Mexico City between 1987 and 1992, followed from birth to 10 years of age
exposure_domain: environmental lead (air lead, lead-glazed ceramics, socioeconomic status, residential location)
limitations: used only three air monitoring stations not necessarily representative of all subjects' residences
lead-glazed ceramic use not quantified and only assessed at study start
potential collinearity between air lead and age
loss to follow-up and incomplete blood lead data
reliance on maternal self-report for pottery use
unable to account for many sources of lead variance
